reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A single larger oval plaque (the herald patch) commonly precedes the widespread eruption by days to a couple of weeks
The secondary rash consists of smaller oval, salmon-coloured plaques with a fine trailing collarette of scale at the inner edge of the border
Lesions align along skin cleavage lines on the trunk, producing the classic Christmas-tree pattern over the back
It is often preceded or accompanied by a mild viral prodrome and is self-limiting, so reassurance is usually the mainstay of management
Symptomatic itch can be eased with emollients, mild topical anti-inflammatory agents, and antihistamines; some evidence supports sunlight or phototherapy for extensive or itchy disease
Because a widespread scaly eruption on the trunk can mimic secondary syphilis, palmar and plantar involvement or risk factors should prompt syphilis serology
Consider a drug-induced pityriasis rosea-like reaction when the history includes a recently started medication or when features are atypical
Counsel pregnant patients appropriately, as some data suggest an association between early-pregnancy disease and adverse outcomes
reference.pathophysiology: Pityriasis rosea is widely regarded as a self-limiting exanthem linked to reactivation of human herpesviruses 6 and 7, supported by the viral prodrome, seasonal clustering, and detection of viral markers in some patients. The eruption reflects a T-cell-mediated inflammatory response in the skin producing spongiotic dermatitis with focal parakeratosis, which accounts for the fine collarette of scale. The alignment of lesions along Langer's cleavage lines gives the distinctive distribution. A clinically indistinguishable pityriasis rosea-like eruption can be triggered by certain drugs and vaccines through a similar hypersensitivity mechanism.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary syphilis (especially with palm and sole involvement)
Tinea corporis (the herald patch can be mistaken for ringworm)
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is clinical based on the herald patch and characteristic distribution
Syphilis serology when the presentation is atypical or there are risk factors, or when palms and soles are involved
Mycology to exclude tinea when a solitary herald patch is uncertain
Review of medication history to identify a possible drug-induced eruption
Skin biopsy reserved for persistent or diagnostically unclear cases
redFlags: Involvement of the palms and soles or a suggestive sexual history pointing to secondary syphilis
Failure to resolve within the expected few months, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Atypical morphology or a temporal link to a new drug suggesting a drug-induced reaction
Early-pregnancy disease, given a possible association with adverse pregnancy outcomes
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, typically clearing over several weeks to a few months without scarring; post-inflammatory pigment change may persist for a while, especially in darker skin, and recurrence is uncommon.
pitfalls: Overlooking secondary syphilis in a widespread scaly truncal eruption
Mistaking the herald patch for tinea and treating with antifungals alone
Failing to link an atypical eruption to a recently started drug
Over-investigating or over-treating a self-limiting condition instead of reassuring the patient
management: Reassurance and explanation that it is a benign, self-limiting eruption resolving over several weeks
Emollients and mild topical corticosteroids to relieve pruritus
Natural sunlight exposure or narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy for extensive or intensely itchy disease
Oral aciclovir considered in early, extensive or severe cases given the herpesvirus association
Review of the drug history to identify a pityriasis rosea-like drug eruption
Syphilis serology when the presentation is atypical or palms and soles are involved
